title: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
summary_raw: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. — Ad

title: Mathematicians say OpenAI doesn't understand its own Navier-Stokes proof
summary_raw: OpenAI submitted a 166-page solution to the Navier-Stokes problem but apparently doesn't fully understand its own proof. Several groups of experts dispute the claimed methodology, saying the actual approach differs from what OpenAI described. And because language models are black boxes, where the underlying ideas came from will likely never be clear. title: China plans to tighten export controls on open-weight models and 23 key AI technologies

title: Is AI interpretability close to a breakthrough? A new essay has researchers divided
summary_raw: Neural networks may be much easier to read than researchers assumed, with about 90 percent of neurons serving a clear function.
